passages.text: For if someone wishing to profess prophecy is allowed to have it believed, in the matters in which he is caught as a liar, that at that time he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge, he will not be easy to expose, though he is a prophet who is a liar. For in the cases where, while saying many things, he hits upon a few, he is then believed to have the spirit. Moreover, he speaks of first things as last and last things as first, things that have happened as things that will happen, and things that will happen as though they had already happened. He also says other, incoherent things, things stolen from others and transformed, and some things curtailed, shapeless, senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear, all loudly proclaiming utter unintelligibility.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ τῆς προγνώσεως ἅγιον οὐκ εἶχεν πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: he did not have the holy spirit of foreknowledge
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the source’s attributive relation between the holy spirit and foreknowledge without imposing a later doctrinal identification.

lexical_decisions.chosen: while saying many things, he hits upon a few
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτυγχάνει describes occasionally hitting the mark or obtaining a correct result among numerous claims.
ὑφαιρέω can mean taking something away secretly; “appropriated from others” is a less pointed alternative.
The perfect passive describes things reduced, diminished, or mutilated; “curtailed” fits the treatment of allegedly defective predictions.
The printed spelling supports ἀνειδής, “without form, shapeless, unsightly,” rather than ἀναιδής, “shameless.”

The main text takes δυσσυνειδησία as difficulty of comprehension, continuing the immediately preceding descriptions senseless, ambiguous, crooked, and unclear. Utter expresses the totality of πάσης, while loudly proclaiming retains the statements' shouting image. The material moral alternative is all loudly proclaiming every kind of guilty conscience, reading the distorted and appropriated statements as exposing their speaker's fraudulent conscience; unscrupulousness is a related moral extension. The surrounding obscurity list favors the comprehension reading, but does not eliminate the moral one.

passages.text: Some of the wicked demons lie in wait in another way. At first they do not even reveal that they exist, so that no effort against them may arise; but at an opportune moment, under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else, they suddenly assault the body by a sword, a noose, a precipice, or some other means. And they bring it about that the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them will be punished to the end, as we said, after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire. Others, being ambushed in another way, do not approach us, because they are deceived by the thoughts of the wicked demons into supposing that they suffer these things from their own gods because of their neglect toward them, that they can reconcile those gods through sacrifices, and that they must not approach us but, on the contrary, must flee and hate us. And they likewise hate and flee those who have greater compassion for them and pursue them in order to benefit them.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν ἀρχὴν οὐδὲ ὅτι εἰσὶν ἐνφαίνοντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: At first they do not even reveal that they exist
lexical_decisions.rationale: τὴν ἀρχήν can mean “at the beginning” or idiomatically “at all”; the subsequent reference to an opportune occasion favors a temporal contrast.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὀργῆς προφάσει, ἔρωτος ἢ ἄλλου τινὸς
lexical_decisions.chosen: under the pretext of anger, erotic passion, or something else
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἔρως here denotes passionate or erotic desire, while πρόφασις presents these emotions as pretexts or occasions.
ἐνυβρίζω conveys violent mistreatment or outrage against the body.

lexical_decisions.chosen: they bring it about that ... will be punished to the end
lexical_decisions.rationale: The future passive participle κολασθησομένας gives the punishment prospective force. εἰς τέλος may mean “to the end,” “completely,” or, in some contexts, “forever”; the source-transparent wording leaves its extent unresolved.

lexical_decisions.chosen: after they—the demons—have entered the purifying fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: χωρήσαντες is nominative masculine plural and most directly resumes the demons as grammatical subject. A contextual association with the people mingled with them is possible despite the case difference.

lexical_decisions.chosen: And they likewise hate and flee
lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected print reads ὁμῶς, ordinarily alike, equally, or likewise. Likewise preserves that sense. The prior English all the same was concessive in context, corresponding to the different customary Greek accentuation ὅμως, nevertheless; that interpretation is not silently imposed or presented as the printed form. No Greek accent correction or OCR defect is claimed.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ἀνακεκραμένων τὰς ἠπατημένας αὐτοῖς ψυχάς
lexical_decisions.chosen: the deceived souls of those who have been mingled with them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main wording attaches αὐτοῖς to the more distant mingling participle, supported by the blending of demons with souls described immediately before in9.11. A material alternative attaches it to the nearer deceived participle: the souls deceived by them, belonging to those who have been mingled. The main text does not claim its longer-distance attachment is uniquely established, and no correction to the supplied Greek is proposed.
